interactions.summary: A student adds Hong Kong feng shui and funerary architecture as another environment saturated with spiritual management practices.
Jiang asks skeptics for objections, and a student argues that demonic-possession language may be a coping mechanism people use when a familiar person commits a shocking sin.
Jiang pivots from possession to whether the Divine Comedy has personally changed the readers, and one student says it can make hidden guilt more conscious.

claims.claim: A student proposes that possession talk may function as a psychological defense against admitting that someone ordinary chose to commit an extreme sin.
Jiang treats the experiential effect of reading the Divine Comedy as the next relevant test case after the possession debate.
A student says the Divine Comedy can surface guilt by forcing attention onto morality that daily life normally numbs or hides.

signature_moments.moment: Possession can be read not as metaphysics but as the story people tell when they cannot bear that a familiar soul chose the evil itself.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It puts a live skeptical psychology inside the lecture instead of leaving the demonic reading unchallenged.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Foreshadowed here as the kind of skeptical psychological explanation Jiang is inviting before the next packet names it explicitly.

chronology_notes.note: The lecture deliberately turns from objective claims about demons to subjective evidence about how the text alters readers.

uncertainty_notes.note: The Hong Kong tomb example is vivid but locally specific and not central to the packet's larger move from possession debate to reader transformation.
